ONE DSD CONSULTANT TWIN
Product Requirements Document for an AI-Native Professional Reasoning and Operational Equity System
Product owner: Independent consultant and creator of the One DSD People, Access and Culture Program
Initial operating context: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Disability Services Division
Product form: Consultant-owned intelligence kernel with configurable staff, pilot, demonstration, and enterprise environments
Autonomy target: 90–95% agent-driven routine program activity, with immediate consultant override and versioned control
Version: 0.1 — Foundational product definition
Date: September 1, 2026
Status: Working draft for consultant review and iterative calibration
Product decision: Build One DSD as a living simulation of the consultant's professional practice: a system that can teach, facilitate, coach, research, analyze, create work products, operate the program, and adapt under the consultant's authority.
Document purpose
This PRD defines the intended product before further feature work. It converts the creator's ambition into an implementable operating model, product architecture, functional requirements, agent autonomy system, evaluation program, pilot plan, and pathway to broader DHS demonstration and adoption.
It supersedes any framing of One DSD as primarily a resource hub, training catalog, or conventional chatbot. Those capabilities remain valuable, but they become components of a larger professional operating system.

Contents
1. Executive product definition
2. Ownership, context, and strategic intent
3. Problem and product thesis
4. Users and operating environments
5. Consultant Twin cognitive architecture
6. Agentic operating model and autonomy
7. Core capability domains
8. End-to-end workflows
9. Functional requirements
10. Nonfunctional requirements

12. Evaluation, calibration, and adaptive evolution
13. Pilot, demonstration, and scale strategy

17. Initial consultant interview agenda
18. Definition of product success

1. Executive product definition
One DSD is a first-of-its-kind, consultant-owned, AI-native operational equity program designed initially for the Disability Services Division and capable of expanding across Minnesota DHS. It is intended to scale the creator's 22 years of DEI/DEIA expertise so staff can receive practical, context-aware assistance at the moment of work without requiring the consultant to personally participate in every interaction.
The system must behave as a coherent professional extension of the consultant. It should reproduce the consultant's philosophy, diagnostic approach, teaching method, facilitation stance, intercultural-development practice, research discipline, operational judgment, and communication style while remaining transparent that it is an AI-enabled consultant-owned resource.
One DSD is not limited to answering questions. It must carry work through a complete cycle: understand the situation, frame the real problem, gather context, retrieve authoritative knowledge, apply multiple perspectives, teach what is needed, generate options, create usable artifacts, record action, follow up, learn from results, and improve through consultant-approved adaptation.
North-star outcome: A staff member, leader, or equity practitioner can enter One DSD at any point in a real work situation and receive the kind of structured, candid, humane, operational assistance they would receive from the consultant—within minutes, at scale, and with continuity over time.
1.1 Product classification
Professional reasoning system: applies expert judgment to ambiguous work rather than merely retrieving content.
Consultant intelligence system: continuously supports research, environmental scanning, sensemaking, learning, and strategic preparation across the full DEIA practice domain.
Operating and implementation system: converts analysis into plans, work products, coordinated actions, facilitated experiences, follow-up, and measurable learning.
Operational practice environment: helps users complete real work products and action cycles.
Learning and facilitation ecosystem: teaches, rehearses, coaches, and supports difficult conversations.
Consultant operating system: gives the creator private control over doctrine, agents, research, content, evaluation, and program operations.
Replicable platform: supports a demonstration environment and later configurations for other equity professionals or DHS-wide use.
1.2 Product boundaries
One DSD may produce complete drafts, analyses, facilitation plans, learning objects, scripts, agendas, communication products, and operational recommendations. The system must distinguish assistance from formal organizational authority: an AI-produced artifact can be complete and useful while still requiring the appropriate person to review, approve, submit, or formally decide.
The product must not confuse caution with incapacity. Its boundaries should preserve privacy, source integrity, lawful authority, and human accountability while allowing bold, substantive, high-value work.
2. Ownership, context, and strategic intent
2.1 Ownership
The program, professional framework, consultant doctrine, system architecture, authored materials, agent behavior profiles, and derivative demonstration environment are consultant-owned intellectual property except where a source retains its own rights.
The product is used in conjunction with the consultant's work with Minnesota DHS; it is not represented as an independently authorized DHS information system unless DHS later adopts it through its own process.
The consultant remains the final product authority and may override, revise, pause, promote, or roll back agent behavior and program content.
The technical design must preserve portability so the consultant can move models, hosting, storage, and delivery channels without losing the brain.
2.2 Strategic intent
The immediate purpose is to create a comprehensive operational program for DSD that can support approximately 180 division staff while drawing on the broader knowledge required to work across a 5,000-plus-person human-services agency. The longer-term purpose is to demonstrate a scalable model for leadership, equity directors, practitioners, and staff at multiple levels.
The product should be experimental by design: model-agnostic, multimodal, voice-capable, adaptive, tool-using, evaluation-driven, and prepared for progressively more capable AI. Experimental does not mean disposable. The architecture must support versioning, evidence, reproducibility, reversibility, and disciplined learning.
2.3 Baseline assets already available
The June 2026 One DSD Brain Export establishes a substantial starting base. It contains 516 knowledge assets, 4,778 searchable chunks and embeddings, 427 learning modules, 74 learning paths, 49 scenarios, 17 worked examples, 81 disciplines, 92 discipline personas, agent specifications, evaluation standards, authority classifications, consultation structures, and voice assets.
Because the program is new, limited historical run data is expected. The initial behavior baseline will be created prospectively through consultant-authored doctrine, scenario simulation, structured critique, pilot interactions, and controlled evaluation—not by treating missing historical traces as missing expertise.
3. Problem and product thesis
3.1 Problem statement
The consultant's expertise is broad, integrative, and operational, but personal availability is finite. Staff need assistance across training, facilitation, intercultural development, coaching, service design, ethnography, culturally responsive practice, disability, accessibility, race, organizational culture, leadership, community engagement, policy, data, and institutional change. Conventional training catalogs and resource libraries cannot reproduce situational judgment at the moment of work.
The practical bottleneck is not a lack of content. It is the inability of one expert to be continuously present across every decision, meeting, design effort, learning need, conflict, and follow-up. One DSD must convert expertise into a durable operating capability without flattening that expertise into generic advice.
3.2 Product thesis
Thesis: If the consultant's professional doctrine, knowledge, judgment patterns, teaching methods, tools, and work-product standards are represented as a versioned cognitive architecture—and agents can apply that architecture to persistent work objects—One DSD can deliver high-fidelity operational consultation at scale while increasing rather than replacing the consultant's strategic reach.
3.3 Consultant intelligence-to-implementation cycle
The Consultant Twin must support the consultant before, during, and after delivery. It should help the consultant research and learn; make sense of a developing issue; design an intervention; create an implementation plan; execute bounded program work; evaluate what happened; and convert the result into future capability.
1. Sense: monitor assigned domains, identify developments, surface emerging questions, and organize incoming materials.
2. Research: gather controlling documents, current evidence, stakeholder perspectives, comparable practice, and unresolved questions.
3. Interpret: explain what changed, what it means, who may be affected, and where legal, operational, cultural, disability, racial, language, or institutional implications intersect.
4. Design: create the intervention, consultation approach, engagement process, learning experience, analytic method, or implementation strategy.
5. Plan: establish outcomes, scope, roles, sequence, resources, communications, accessibility, risks, measures, and decision points.
6. Execute: generate work products, coordinate bounded tasks, facilitate or support delivery, track commitments, and adapt to conditions.
7. Evaluate: collect evidence, participant feedback, outcomes, surprises, gaps, and implementation lessons.
8. Learn and adapt: update the work object, propose program improvements, strengthen evaluation cases, and prepare the next cycle for consultant approval.
Operating requirement: The product must be able to move from intelligence to implementation. Research that does not improve a decision, plan, learning experience, engagement process, or work product is incomplete.
3.4 What the product must not become
A static DEI website with an AI search box.
A generic chatbot wearing One DSD colors.
A collection of disconnected specialist bots with inconsistent judgment or voice.
A course catalog that mistakes completion for application.
A system that over-refuses useful work or hides behind disclaimers.
A self-modifying agent that changes the consultant's philosophy without review.
A DHS-branded fork that causes the consultant-owned core to fragment.
4. Users and operating environments
Environment
Primary users
Purpose
Data posture
Consultant OS
Program owner
Author doctrine, calibrate agents, build learning, review patterns, operate the ecosystem, override any action
Private consultant data and full control plane
DSD Pilot
Selected DSD staff and leaders
Use the system on real, appropriately bounded work; generate pilot evidence and corrections
Authenticated pilot workspace with separated work objects
Leadership Demo
DHS leadership, equity directors, practitioners
Demonstrate the same product kernel through realistic synthetic scenarios and seeded data
No live staff records; resettable demonstration tenant
Enterprise / Practitioner

Configure the kernel for broader agency use or another practitioner's doctrine
Tenant-specific knowledge, policies, identities, and evaluation


These environments should be configurations of one product kernel, not divergent code copies. Models, tools, doctrine, data sources, permissions, and branding may vary by environment, but fixes and core improvements should move through one governed release process.
4.1 Primary user groups
Consultant/program owner: authors, teaches, governs, evaluates, researches, and supervises adaptive behavior.
Frontline and operational staff: need immediate help applying equity, access, culture, and disability practice to ordinary work.
Supervisors and managers: need support with people decisions, difficult conversations, team culture, change, and accountability.
Program, policy, data, communications, procurement, and service-design staff: need structured analysis and work-product assistance.
Executives and senior leaders: need concise strategic analysis, scenario planning, risk awareness, and implementation options.
Equity professionals: need advanced practitioner tools, program design, facilitation, curriculum development, and critical thought partnership.
Learning participants: need multimodal, accessible, practice-based learning tied to real work moments.
5. Consultant Twin cognitive architecture
Every agent capability must inherit a shared Consultant Twin kernel. Specialized agents may perform different tasks, but they must not invent independent philosophies or personas. Users should experience one coherent professional intelligence.
Constitution. Ownership, purpose, values, non-negotiables, voice, intellectual stance, boundaries, and the consultant's definition of useful practice.
Knowledge. The governed One DSD corpus, current authoritative sources, consultant-created frameworks, multimedia, and research extensions.
Practice protocols. Repeatable methods for analysis, facilitation, coaching, intercultural development, research, service design, learning design, and follow-through.
Judgment model. Cues, diagnostic questions, competing perspectives, failure patterns, tradeoffs, uncertainty, escalation thresholds, and what the consultant notices first.
Work memory. Persistent work objects, decisions, drafts, sources, actions, outcomes, feedback, and next-review dates.
Teaching model. How the consultant explains, sequences, challenges, rehearses, differentiates, and turns theory into applied performance.
Relational model. How tone, pacing, candor, empathy, cultural humility, authority, and resistance are handled in context.
Evaluation model. How fidelity, usefulness, evidence, learning, accessibility, and appropriate autonomy are measured and improved.
5.1 Persistent work object
The primary unit of the product is not the webpage or chat transcript. It is a persistent object representing a real episode of work. Conversation, learning, research, analysis, artifacts, actions, and follow-up become views on that object.
Identity: title, owner, team, role, work type, status, and dates.
Situation: current facts, desired outcome, constraints, urgency, and decision authority.
People and systems: affected groups, communities, stakeholders, power relationships, service interfaces, and institutional context.
Reasoning: initial frame, diagnostic questions, assumptions, evidence, perspectives, options, tradeoffs, uncertainties, and recommendation.
Practice: relevant learning moments, facilitation or coaching steps, and consultant methods applied.
Production: drafts, analyses, agendas, scripts, plans, learning objects, reports, and export formats.
Action and memory: commitments, owners, due dates, outcomes, feedback, review date, and lessons promoted to the brain.
5.2 Memory system
Semantic memory: what the program knows.
Procedural memory: how the program performs professional tasks.
Episodic memory: what happened in prior deidentified work episodes and what was learned.
Preference memory: documented consultant and user preferences that improve delivery without stereotyping.
Institutional memory: deidentified patterns across work, needs, outcomes, and repeated barriers.
Developmental memory: how a user, team, or organizational capability is progressing over time where the use is appropriate and consented.
6. Agentic operating model and autonomy
6.1 Autonomy objective
The product target is for agents to perform 90–95% of routine program activity by volume. This includes intake, retrieval, analysis preparation, teaching, drafting, formatting, accessibility checks, routing, reminders, content maintenance proposals, evaluation runs, pattern analysis, and preparation of consultant review packets.
The remaining human-controlled activity should be defined by consequence rather than workload. The consultant retains authority over doctrine, public positioning, high-impact professional judgments, formal approvals, disputed interpretations, behavior promotion, and any action the consultant designates for review.
Level
Agent authority
Typical One DSD use
Consultant control

Read, classify, summarize, and identify patterns

6.2 Coherent agent system
The preferred architecture is one principal Consultant Twin orchestrator with tool-using specialist capabilities. Specialist components should be introduced because a task requires distinct context, evaluation, or tools—not because a multi-agent diagram appears sophisticated.
Research and evidence capability
Equity analysis and work-product capability
Training and e-learning design capability
Facilitation and hard-conversation capability
Intercultural development and coaching capability
Ethnography, service design, and culturally responsive practice capability
Leadership, organizational culture, and change capability
Accessibility, disability, and language-access capability
Program operations, measurement, and adaptive-learning capability
Quality, sensitivity, source, and fidelity evaluation capability
6.3 Override and control requirements
Global pause and per-agent pause controls.
Per-tool permissions and limits by environment, user, task, and risk class.
Preview, approve, edit, reject, regenerate, and roll-back controls.
Versioned doctrine, prompts, tools, models, evaluation sets, and behavior releases.
Readable activity histories that explain sources, tools, assumptions, and decision path without exposing hidden chain-of-thought.
Candidate-learning queue where agents propose improvements but cannot silently change production behavior.
Consultant-set autonomy budgets, escalation rules, and emergency shutdown.
7. Core capability domains
Consultant intelligence and implementation
Research, synthesize, plan, and help execute DEIA work across legislative, policy, program, organizational, workforce, service, learning, and community contexts.
Maintain issue dossiers, stakeholder maps, implementation plans, decision calendars, research questions, work products, and follow-up in persistent work objects.
Act as the consultant's planning and production partner while preserving the consultant's final authority over priorities, positions, and high-consequence decisions.
Operational DEI/DEIA practice
Apply equity to policy, programs, services, people practices, budgets, communications, procurement, and operations.
Distinguish symbolic activity, compliance, inclusion, equity, anti-racism, multicultural practice, and transformational change.
Translate concepts into decisions, behaviors, work products, measures, and follow-through.
Training and e-learning
Design complete curricula, microlearning, scenario learning, facilitator guides, knowledge checks, reflective practice, and accessible multimedia.
Adapt depth, pace, modality, examples, and practice to audience role, readiness, time, and work context.
Generate instructor and learner materials while preserving the consultant's teaching philosophy.
Facilitation and hard conversations
Prepare agendas, openings, agreements, questions, likely tensions, interventions, repair moves, and follow-up.
Support live or simulated facilitation without pretending conflict can be solved by a script alone.
Help users rehearse difficult conversations and receive developmental feedback.
Intercultural development and coaching
Support developmental learning, reflection, perspective shifting, communication adaptation, and coaching plans.
Connect intercultural development to actual service, supervision, leadership, and organizational practice.
Keep licensed assessments or proprietary instruments within the consultant's authorized use and configuration.
Ethnography and culturally responsive services
Design listening, observation, qualitative inquiry, journey mapping, service ethnography, and community-informed research.
Convert findings into service-design decisions, not cultural stereotypes or static profiles.
Teach staff to distinguish general cultural context from the person, family, or community in front of them.
Disability, access, and human services
Integrate disability rights, disability justice, accessibility, language access, person-centered practice, Olmstead, HCBS, and service quality.
Use the comprehensive DHS context required by DSD rather than treating disability services as isolated.
Connect workforce, community, policy, technology, and service-delivery implications.
Leadership and organizational change
Coach leaders through resistance, polarization, accountability, systems thinking, culture, power, trust, and implementation.
Distinguish individual conflict from organizational patterns and structural incentives.
Create strategic options, decision briefs, change plans, leadership learning, and feedback loops.
Research and field intelligence
Maintain authoritative source hierarchies and current research extensions.
Separate official requirements, credible research, consultant synthesis, inference, and emerging experimentation.
Turn research into program updates, learning, tools, and testable practices.
8. End-to-end workflows
8.1 Universal operational consultation cycle
1. Receive the user's situation in natural language, voice, document, image, or selected work context.
2. Determine the real work type, desired outcome, urgency, decision authority, and missing context.
3. Ask a small number of high-value diagnostic questions in the consultant's style.
4. Retrieve the relevant consultant doctrine, program materials, official sources, prior patterns, and work-object memory.
5. Run the required perspectives: people affected, access, culture, disability, race, language, power, systems, evidence, implementation, and accountability as relevant.
6. Teach only what the user needs to understand the work and make a better decision.
7. Generate options, tradeoffs, recommendation, uncertainty, and the consequences of inaction.
8. Produce the requested artifact or next action in an editable, accessible form.
9. Record decisions, actions, owners, dates, feedback, and follow-up in the work object.
10. Evaluate the interaction and promote only consultant-approved lessons into future behavior.
8.2 Priority vertical slices
Legislative proposal or bill analysis: from bill text and research through provision mapping, equity implications, stakeholder analysis, implementation considerations, briefing products, questions, and follow-up monitoring.
Policy and procedure change: from initial proposal through analysis, engagement, options, decision brief, implementation, and review.
Engagement event: from purpose and stakeholder mapping through relationship strategy, accessible logistics, facilitation, participation methods, documentation, report-back, and continued engagement.
Staff learning circle: from performance need through sequence, readings or media, agreements, prompts, activities, facilitation notes, reflective practice, evaluation, and transfer to work.
Hard conversation or team conflict: from situation diagnosis through rehearsal, facilitation plan, live support, repair, and follow-up.
Culturally responsive service design: from problem framing through ethnographic inquiry, accessibility and intercultural analysis, prototype, feedback, and implementation.
Training request: from performance problem through learning objectives, instructional strategy, scenarios, multimedia, facilitation materials, evaluation, and revision.
Intercultural coaching: from developmental need through reflection, practice plan, rehearsal, evidence of adaptation, and next-stage learning.
General DEIA consultation: from unstructured question through diagnosis, evidence, professional judgment, options, recommendation, work product, action, and follow-up.
8.3 Legislative proposal and bill analysis workflow
1. Acquire and version the bill, amendment, fiscal note, analysis, testimony, related law or policy, and authoritative background.
2. Create a plain-language provision map identifying what changes, who has authority, relevant dates, dependencies, and unresolved interpretation questions.
3. Analyze affected populations, disability and access, race and ethnicity, language, geography, Tribal and government-to-government implications, workforce, providers, counties, service systems, administrative burden, and likely unintended effects as relevant.
4. Distinguish documented effects from plausible hypotheses and identify the data or engagement needed to resolve uncertainty.
5. Map supporters, opponents, implementers, affected communities, decision-makers, and the strongest good-faith arguments on each side.
6. Develop implementation scenarios, risk controls, communication needs, engagement strategy, learning implications, and measures.
7. Produce a configurable package: executive brief, detailed bill analysis, equity-impact questions, stakeholder map, implementation checklist, talking points, and monitoring plan.
8. Track amendments and new evidence, compare versions, and alert the consultant to material changes requiring reassessment.
8.4 Engagement event workflow
1. Clarify whether the purpose is informing, listening, consulting, co-designing, deciding, repairing, or sustaining a relationship.
2. Identify whose participation is essential, who holds decision authority, who is usually absent, and what prior relationships or harms shape the event.
3. Design access, language, disability, timing, location, technology, transportation, compensation, food, childcare, sensory, and participation supports proportionately.
4. Create outreach, invitations, registration, pre-reads, facilitator scripts, activities, decision points, documentation methods, and contingency plans.
5. Support facilitation and real-time adaptation without reducing participation to a performance or extracting community input without response.
6. Produce an accessible report-back showing what was heard, what will change, what will not change and why, who owns next actions, and when participants will hear back.
8.5 Staff learning-circle workflow
1. Identify the performance, relationship, or practice problem the circle is intended to improve.
2. Design a developmental sequence using readings, audio, scenarios, reflection, dialogue, practice, and application to participants' work.
3. Create facilitator guidance for openings, agreements, difficult moments, uneven participation, defensiveness, emotional impact, repair, and closure.
4. Adapt the learning circle by role, readiness, accessibility, cultural context, group history, time, and organizational conditions.
5. Capture commitments and application without turning reflection into surveillance.
6. Evaluate transfer into work and use the evidence to improve the next learning cycle.
9. Functional requirements
FR-001 — Unified intake. Accept natural-language, voice, file, and form-based intake and convert it into a structured work object.
FR-002 — Context diagnosis. Identify role, work type, intended outcome, affected people, authority, urgency, constraints, and missing information.
FR-003 — Consultant-style questioning. Select a small number of high-value questions based on the consultant's diagnostic method rather than a fixed generic form.
FR-004 — Grounded retrieval. Search by meaning and filter by authority, audience, domain, date, format, work type, and environment.
FR-005 — Multi-perspective reasoning. Apply relevant equity, disability, access, cultural, racial, language, systems, power, evidence, and implementation perspectives.
FR-006 — Evidence distinctions. Clearly distinguish source fact, policy requirement, consultant doctrine, synthesis, inference, uncertainty, and recommendation.
FR-007 — Work-product generation. Produce complete editable artifacts in common office, web, audio, and learning formats.
FR-008 — Persistent workspaces. Save, resume, branch, compare, archive, and review work objects across sessions.
FR-009 — Teaching in the work. Insert just-in-time instruction, examples, rehearsal, and practice directly into a live task.
FR-010 — Facilitation mode. Prepare and support hard conversations, workshops, meetings, and debriefs with adaptable plans and interventions.
FR-011 — Coaching mode. Support reflection, developmental practice, feedback, goal-setting, rehearsal, and follow-up without flattening people into types.
FR-012 — Research mode. Conduct current, source-verifiable research and convert findings into actionable program intelligence.
FR-013 — Program operations. Run bounded content, learning, accessibility, evaluation, reporting, and maintenance workflows.
FR-014 — Multimodal delivery. Use the established podcast voices, individual read-aloud voices, transcripts, visuals, documents, and interactive learning where appropriate.
FR-015 — Consultant review studio. Let the consultant inspect, compare, correct, annotate, approve, reject, and promote outputs and behavior changes.
FR-016 — Adaptive learning. Create candidate lessons from interaction and evaluation evidence; require versioned promotion and support rollback.
FR-017 — Autonomy control. Provide global, agent, workflow, tool, environment, and risk-level control over autonomous action.
FR-018 — Demonstration tenant. Create resettable synthetic scenarios that demonstrate the full product without exposing live pilot data.
FR-019 — Configuration and cloning. Support a shared kernel with tenant-specific doctrine, knowledge, agents, users, branding, permissions, and evaluation.
FR-020 — Outcome follow-up. Track commitments, outcomes, review dates, user feedback, consultant corrections, and institutional patterns.
FR-021 — Legislative intelligence. Ingest, version, compare, research, and analyze legislative proposals, bills, amendments, fiscal notes, testimony, and related authoritative material.
FR-022 — Policy intelligence. Analyze proposed or existing policy across authority, intent, implementation, equity effects, access, affected groups, evidence, stakeholder perspectives, and operational consequences.
FR-023 — Implementation planning. Convert findings into sequenced plans with outcomes, owners, resources, dependencies, risks, accessibility, communications, measures, and review points.
FR-024 — Engagement operations. Design and support engagement events from relationship strategy and accessible logistics through facilitation, report-back, commitments, and continued engagement.
FR-025 — Learning-circle operations. Design, facilitate, adapt, document, and evaluate recurring staff learning circles tied to practice and transfer.
FR-026 — Consultant intelligence workspace. Maintain issue dossiers, research queues, planning boards, decision calendars, stakeholder maps, briefing packages, and implementation status across the consultant's portfolio.
FR-027 — Change monitoring. Track assigned legislative, policy, research, organizational, or program developments and surface only material changes with an explanation of why they matter.
10. Nonfunctional requirements
Fidelity: behavior must be measurable against the consultant's approved doctrine, examples, critiques, and evaluation cases.
Model portability: provider adapters and capability profiles must prevent hard dependence on one model or vendor.
Accessibility: staff-facing and consultant-facing experiences, documents, audio, captions, transcripts, keyboard operation, and contrast must be designed for accessibility from the start.
Privacy separation: consultant-private, pilot, demonstration, and future tenant data must remain technically and operationally separable.
Traceability: outputs must retain source, model, tool, version, work-object, and approval history sufficient for review and rollback.
Resilience: the system must fail clearly, preserve work, and degrade to retrieval or deterministic workflows when a reasoning provider is unavailable.
Performance: routine interactions should begin streaming quickly; complex workflows should show meaningful progress and allow continuation.
Comprehensibility: users should understand recommendations, sources, uncertainty, and next steps without seeing internal implementation jargon.
Reversibility: agent-created changes must be undoable where technically possible, with snapshots before material changes.
Evolution: models, tools, and behavior releases must be replaceable without rebuilding the program's intellectual core.
11. Knowledge, content, and research program
11.1 Source hierarchy
1. Consultant doctrine and authored intellectual framework
2. Controlling law, policy, official DHS and Minnesota sources
3. Approved One DSD program assets and operational protocols
4. Peer-reviewed and institutionally reviewed research
5. Credible field practice and external toolkits
6. Deidentified pilot evidence and consultant-approved practice lessons
7. Clearly labeled experimental synthesis and hypotheses
11.2 Prospective expertise capture
Because the product is new, the consultant twin will be calibrated prospectively. The consultant's authority is not contingent on historical application logs. Instead, the program will deliberately create the examples and evaluations needed to translate expertise into machine-actionable behavior.
Professional doctrine interviews covering philosophy, distinctions, non-negotiables, voice, and definitions of good work.
Critical-incident interviews covering difficult real situations, decisive cues, rejected options, tradeoffs, and lessons.
Simulated consultation sessions across representative DHS scenarios.
Contrastive critique: the consultant compares alternative agent responses and explains why one is stronger.
Artifact calibration: examples of weak, acceptable, strong, and exceptional work products.
Live pilot corrections converted into versioned evaluation cases and candidate behavior updates.
11.3 Research agenda
Map the full practitioner capability universe and identify where the consultant's approach is distinctive.
Observe and interview staff about real work moments, cognitive load, common failures, and preferred assistance.
Maintain current research across DEI/DEIA, disability, intercultural communication, adult learning, ethnography, culturally responsive services, organizational change, public administration, and agentic AI.
Test learning transfer and operational outcomes, not only user satisfaction or course completion.
Use external programs as research inputs rather than design ceilings or templates.
12. Evaluation, calibration, and adaptive evolution
12.1 Evaluation dimensions
Dimension
Core question
Evidence
Consultant fidelity
Would the consultant recognize and endorse the reasoning, stance, and recommendation?
Blind rankings, critique agreement, doctrine adherence
Problem recognition
Did the system identify the real operational problem and missing context?
Scenario gold labels and consultant review
Operational utility
Can the user act, decide, teach, facilitate, or produce better work?
Task completion, artifact quality, follow-through
Learning effectiveness
Did the interaction improve capability beyond the immediate answer?
Rehearsal, transfer task, later performance
Evidence quality
Are sources appropriate, current, accurately represented, and distinguishable from inference?
Retrieval and citation checks
Relational quality
Did the system use appropriate candor, warmth, pacing, challenge, humility, and power awareness?
Consultant and participant ratings
Autonomy quality
Did the system act at the correct level, stop when needed, and preserve override?
Tool, workflow, exception, and rollback tests
Equity and access
Did it identify burdens, exclusions, disability, language, culture, race, power, and downstream effects proportionately?
Adversarial and edge-case evaluations


12.2 Adaptive behavior lifecycle
1. Observe a pattern in deidentified interaction, evaluation, research, or consultant correction data.
2. Generate a candidate lesson with supporting evidence and the affected behavior components.
3. Simulate the change against the relevant evaluation suite and known edge cases.
4. Present the before/after behavior, benefits, regressions, and uncertainties to the consultant.
5. Consultant approves, revises, rejects, or requests more evidence.
6. Promote the approved behavior as a versioned release with rollback capability.
7. Monitor the release and add real failures or surprises to the evaluation corpus.
Adaptive principle: The system may learn continuously, but it may not silently redefine the consultant. Adaptation is evidence-driven, testable, versioned, and reversible.
12.3 Initial success thresholds
At least 90% pass rate on consultant-defined must-pass fidelity scenarios before staff pilot expansion.
Zero unresolved hard failures on privacy, fabricated authority, source invention, or destructive autonomous actions.
At least 85% of pilot users can complete the target work episode without direct consultant intervention.
At least 80% of reviewed work products are usable with light rather than structural revision.
Consultant agrees that the system asked the right diagnostic questions in at least 90% of sampled complex cases.
Agent-driven handling reaches 90–95% of routine program activity by volume without increasing critical-error rates.
13. Pilot, demonstration, and scale strategy
13.1 Consultant alpha
Consultant uses the system alone against authentic, deidentified work and deliberately difficult simulations.
Every disagreement becomes a structured critique or evaluation case.
No capability is called complete because it produces impressive prose; it must complete the professional workflow.
13.2 Small staff pilot
Recruit a small, varied group representing different roles, confidence levels, and work types.
Pilot three to five complete workflows rather than the entire theoretical capability universe.
Measure whether users complete work, improve judgment, need rescue, trust sources, and return successfully.
Review pilot interactions with the consultant and convert findings into behavior and product changes.
13.3 Leadership and equity-professional demonstration
The demonstration environment should run the same product kernel and agent behavior release as the pilot, but with synthetic users, synthetic work objects, resettable scenarios, and no access to live staff data. The demonstration should show complete episodes of work, including the system's ability to diagnose, teach, create, remember, adapt, and escalate.
13.4 Scale path
DSD operational program

17. Initial consultant interview agenda
The first interview cycle should establish the professional constitution before attempting to capture every possible case. The consultant is the authoritative source for the product's initial doctrine; testing refines implementation rather than adjudicating whether the consultant possesses expertise.
1. What must One DSD believe about equity, disability, access, culture, power, learning, and public service?
2. What recurring mistakes distinguish superficial DEI work from competent and exceptional practice?
3. When a person brings you a problem, what do you listen for before deciding what they need?
4. How do you decide whether to teach, coach, facilitate, research, challenge, draft, or escalate?
5. What does your best training do that conventional DEI training fails to do?
6. What does culturally responsive service mean operationally at DHS—not rhetorically?
7. What are the most important tensions that cannot be reduced to a checklist?
8. What should the system be capable of doing independently from day one, and what should earn greater autonomy through evidence?
9. What would make you say, without reservation, 'this behaves like me at my professional best'?
18. Definition of product success
Success: One DSD succeeds when it can carry a real episode of equity-related work from uncertainty to informed action in a way the consultant recognizes as faithful, staff experience as practical, and the program can repeat, evaluate, and improve without requiring the consultant to personally perform every step.
The product is not complete when every planned page exists. It is complete enough to scale when the consultant trusts the cognitive architecture, users can produce better work, the system demonstrates measurable learning and operational value, autonomy remains controllable, and improvements compound through evidence rather than drift.
